planting.note: Set out nursery divisions once night temperatures stay above 60°F, in a humus-rich, well-drained container mix or shaded bed; keep the swollen petiole bases above the soil line.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade with high humidity, letting the top inch of mix dry between waterings. Philodendron martianum is a non-climbing, self-heading species from Espirito Santo, Brazil, prized for its glossy, upright, spade-shaped leaves and unusually thick, fleshy, water-storing petioles that give the plant its 'Fat Boy' nickname. It is slower and more compact than most large-leaf philodendrons, making it well suited to a shaded patio container or protected understory planting in zone 10-11. Feed lightly during the warm growing season and protect from any temperature below 50°F.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Pot up divisions or nursery starts in spring once temperatures are reliably warm, using a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix; provide a moss pole or allow it to sprawl as a semi-epiphytic understory plant.

directions: Site in bright indirect to moderate shade in a chunky, fast-draining mix, watering thoroughly and then letting the surface dry slightly before the next watering. Philodendron pastazanum is an Ecuadorian species valued for its large, heart-shaped, leathery leaves with a subtly quilted texture and pale, prominent venation that becomes more pronounced as leaves mature. It behaves as a semi-epiphytic understory plant, tolerating deep shade but producing its largest leaves with a few hours of bright, filtered light. In zone 10-11 it can be grown outdoors in a protected, shaded bed or container that is moved under cover below 55°F.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring in rich, well-drained, organic soil in deep to partial shade; established clumps tolerate brief cool snaps better than most collector anthuriums.

directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, mulching well to protect surface roots. Anthurium schlechtendalii is a robust, clumping terrestrial species native from Mexico through Central America, forming large, leathery, paddle-shaped leaves on stout petioles and producing green spathes with a slender, twisted spadix. It is noticeably tougher and more cold- and sun-tolerant than the velvet-leaf collector anthuriums, making it a practical structural foliage plant for shaded Gulf Coast beds in zone 9-11. All plant parts contain calcium oxalate and are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or set out rooted starts in spring in a well-drained, peat-based potting mix; grows well in hanging baskets or as a shaded groundcover in frost-free zones.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in a well-drained, slightly moisture-retentive mix, allowing the surface to dry between waterings to avoid stem rot. Peperomia puteolata, native to Peru and Ecuador, forms a lax, trailing clump of wiry, dark red stems set with narrow, lance-shaped leaves marked with pale parallel stripes running from base to tip, giving rise to its common name. It is compact and shallow-rooted, making it well suited to shallow pots, mixed shade containers, or as a small-scale groundcover accent in protected zone 10-11 gardens. Pinch stem tips occasionally to keep growth dense.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring and plant in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade with high humidity.

directions: Grow in partial to deep shade with consistently moist soil and high ambient humidity; brown leaf edges signal air that is too dry or water that is too mineral-laden. Ctenanthe lubbersiana, native to eastern Brazil, produces long-stalked, lance-shaped leaves irregularly splashed and mottled with cream, pale green, and yellow variegation over a darker green base, giving the clump a mosaic-like appearance distinct from its solid-leaved relatives. Like other prayer-plant relatives, its leaves rise and fold at night. In zone 10-11 it makes an excellent understory accent in a shaded, sheltered bed or large container.

planting.note: Divide clumps or plant nursery starts in spring in a rich, well-drained potting mix in deep shade; this low, spreading species suits shaded groundcover use in frost-free areas as well as indoor pots.

directions: Grow in deep to partial shade in evenly moist, well-drained soil, protecting from any temperature below 55°F. Aglaonema costatum is a low, clumping, stemless species native to the understory forests of Malaysia and Borneo, with broad, dark green, heart-shaped leaves densely speckled in white and a distinctive ivory-white midrib running the length of each leaf. It stays noticeably more compact and ground-hugging than the taller, cane-forming Aglaonema commutatum, making it useful as a small-scale shaded groundcover or foreground accent. It tolerates lower light than almost any other aroid grown for foliage.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings or set out rooted starts in spring; the trailing stems root readily wherever they touch moist soil, making it fast to fill in as a shaded groundcover or hanging basket.

directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in evenly moist, organically rich soil; the trailing, self-rooting stems fill in quickly and tolerate light foot traffic once established. Pilea nummulariifolia, native to the West Indies and northern South America, produces round, coin-shaped, crinkled green leaves along creeping, wiry stems, giving it its common name and a texture distinct from the more upright, silver-patterned Pilea cadierei. In zone 10-11 it works well as a fast shaded groundcover under trees or spilling from a shaded hanging basket; farther north it is grown as an easily propagated houseplant.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Mount pups or nursery divisions on a bark slab or wire basket packed with sphagnum moss in spring; this species tolerates more direct sun and drier air than most staghorn ferns.

directions: Mount on bark or in a wire basket in bright, filtered light to partial sun, watering thoroughly and letting the mount dry before rewetting. Platycerium veitchii, native to inland Queensland, Australia, is covered in a dense coat of silvery-white hairs that give the upright, deeply divided fertile fronds a distinctive frosted appearance and help it withstand more sun and lower humidity than other staghorn ferns. Sterile shield fronds clasp the mount and gradually build up a basket of trapped debris that feeds the plant. In zone 9-11 it can be grown outdoors mounted in a bright, partly shaded spot and brought under cover if temperatures approach freezing.
